title: Big-O Thinking
description: Predict how code slows down as data grows — the one idea behind most performance decisions in programming.
keyIdeas: Big-O describes how work **grows** as input grows, not exact speed.
Drop constants and smaller terms: 3n² + 5n + 2 is O(n²).
One loop over n → O(n). Nested loops → O(n²). Halving each step → O(log n).
Hash maps turn repeated O(n) searches into O(1) lookups (on average).
Efficient sorting is O(n log n). Optimize only where n is actually big.

lessons.title: What Big-O measures
lessons.takeaway: Big-O is the growth shape: keep the dominant term, drop constants, and ask 'what happens when n doubles?'

steps.title: Growth, not speed
steps.body:
When an algorithm handles more data, how much more work does it do? **Big-O notation** describes that *growth rate* as the input size **n** gets large.

We don't care about exact milliseconds (those depend on the machine). We care about the **shape**: if n doubles, does the work stay the same, double, or quadruple?

steps.title: Drop the noise
steps.body:
Big-O keeps only the fastest-growing term and ignores constant factors:

- 3n + 5 → **O(n)**
- n² + 100n → **O(n²)**
- 42 → **O(1)**

For large n, the biggest term dominates everything else.

steps.explanation: Keep the dominant term (n²) and drop the constant factor 5 → **O(n²)**.

steps.title: Doubling the input
steps.problem: An O(n²) algorithm takes 1 second for 1,000 items. Roughly how long for 2,000 items?
steps: Work grows like n². Going from n to 2n multiplies the work by (2n)² ÷ n² = **4**.
steps.answer: About **4 seconds**. Doubling the input quadruples the time.

steps.prompt: An O(n²) algorithm takes 2 seconds for 10,000 items. Roughly how many **seconds** for 100,000 items?
steps.hint: The input grew 10×. What does that do to n²?

steps.prompt: An O(n) algorithm takes 3 s on some input. If the input doubles, roughly how long will it take?
steps.explanation: Linear growth: double the input, double the time → **6 s**.

steps.title: Race: O(n) vs O(n²)
steps.body:
Say each operation takes 1 microsecond. Tap **1,000**: O(n) needs 1,000 operations (1 ms) and O(n²) needs 1,000,000 (1 s). Both feel fine.

Now tap **1,000,000**. O(n) takes 1 second. O(n²) needs a trillion operations: about **12 days**. Same machine, same data; only the growth rate differs.

Switch to the **Log** scale to fit both bars on screen at once.

lessons.title: The five classes you'll meet most
lessons.takeaway: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²). At a million items, that's the difference between instant and forever.

steps.title: The usual suspects
steps.body:
From slowest-growing to fastest-growing:

- **O(1)** constant — reading an array element, a hash map lookup
- **O(log n)** logarithmic — binary search
- **O(n)** linear — one pass over the data
- **O(n log n)** — efficient sorting
- **O(n²)** quadratic — comparing every pair

For n = 1,000,000: log n ≈ 20, n log n ≈ 20 million, and n² = 1 trillion.

steps.title: Why log n is so small
steps.body:
**Binary search** finds an item in a *sorted* list by checking the middle, then throwing away the half that can't contain it — again and again.

How many halvings take n down to 1? That's log₂ n. Each time the data **doubles**, binary search needs just **one** more step.

steps.prompt: About how many steps does binary search need, in the worst case, to search **1,000,000** sorted items? (whole number)
Binary search throws away half the data each step. Watch `n` halve and predict the values when asked.
steps.code:
n = 16
steps = 0
while n > 1:
    n = n // 2
    steps += 1
print(steps)

frames.note: Half of the data is gone after one step.

steps.explanation: 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1 takes 4 halvings, and log₂ 16 = 4. Start from 32 and you need only **one** more step. That's why O(log n) barely grows: doubling the input adds a single step.
steps.hint: `//` divides and drops the remainder: 16 // 2 is 8.

steps.title: All five, side by side
steps.body:
Drag n up to **1,000,000** and compare, at 1 µs per operation:

- O(log n), binary search: about **20** steps, 20 µs. Feels instant.
- O(n log n), a good sort: about 20 million operations, **20 s**.
- O(n²), comparing every pair: a trillion operations, about **12 days**.

Notice how little the O(log n) bar moves as n grows: doubling n adds just one step.

steps.prompt: Which list goes from slowest-growing to fastest-growing?
choices: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²)

steps.prompt: Your input has 10 million items and you need an answer within a few seconds. A typical machine does roughly 100 million simple operations per second. Which complexity is feasible?
steps.explanation: n log n ≈ 10⁷ × 23 ≈ 2.3 × 10⁸ operations — a couple of seconds. n² = 10¹⁴ operations would take over a week.

steps.prompt: What's the typical Big-O of an efficient general-purpose sorting algorithm (like merge sort)? Write it like O(...).
steps.explanation: **O(n log n)** — merge sort, heapsort, and the built-in sort in most languages. No comparison-based sort can do better in general.

steps.title: Bonus: the one to avoid, O(2ⁿ)
steps.body:
One more class worth recognising: **O(2ⁿ)**, exponential. The work **doubles every time n grows by 1** — for example, trying every subset of n items.

At n = 30 that's about a billion operations (**18 min** at 1 µs each). At n = 64 it's about **585,000 years**, while O(n²) at n = 64 is 4,096 operations: 4 ms. Exponential algorithms only work for tiny inputs.

lessons.title: Reading complexity from code
lessons.takeaway: Count the loops: sequential → add, nested → multiply, halving → log. Watch for hidden loops inside library calls.

steps.title: Follow the loops
steps.body:
Most of the time you can read complexity straight off the loops:

- **One loop over n items** → O(n)
- **A loop inside a loop**, both over n → O(n²)
- **Loops one after another** → add them: O(n) + O(n) = O(n)
- **Halving (or doubling) each iteration** → O(log n)

steps.prompt:
What's the complexity of this function?

```
def total(nums):
    s = 0
    for x in nums:
        s += x
    return s
```
steps.explanation: One pass, constant work per item → **O(n)**.
Every pair gets compared: about n²/2 comparisons → **O(n²)**. (The /2 is a constant, so it's dropped.)

steps.prompt: With `n = 3`, count how often the inner line runs. Step through and predict `steps` when asked.

frames.note: First pass of the outer loop: `j` starts at 0.
`j` reached the end of `range(3)`, so the inner loop is done for `i = 0`.
`i` moved on, and the inner loop starts over from `j = 0`.

steps.explanation: The inner loop runs all `n` times **for each** pass of the outer loop, so the body runs n × n = 9 times. Double `n` to 6 and it runs 36 times: four times the work. That's O(n²).
steps.hint: For every value of `i`, `j` goes through 0, 1, 2 again.

steps.prompt:
What's the complexity of this function?

```
def count_halvings(n):
    steps = 0
    while n > 1:
        n = n // 2
        steps += 1
    return steps
```
steps.explanation: n is halved every iteration, so the loop runs about log₂ n times → **O(log n)**.

steps.title: Loops in sequence
steps.problem:
What's the total complexity?

```
for x in nums:          # loop A
    print(x)
for x in nums:          # loop B
    for y in nums:
        print(x, y)
```
steps: Loop B: n × n iterations → O(n²).
They run one after the other, so add: O(n) + O(n²).

steps.prompt:
Watch for hidden loops! In Python, `x in some_list` scans the list item by item. What's the complexity here?

```
for x in a:        # a has n items
    if x in b:     # b is a list of n items
        print(x)
```
steps.explanation: `x in b` is itself an O(n) scan, done n times → **O(n²)**. Turning `b` into a set makes each check O(1), and the whole thing O(n).

steps.prompt: `nums`, `a` and `b` are lists of n items, `sorted_nums` is a sorted list, `seen` is a set and `d` is a dict. Sort each line by its complexity.

items.text: `[x for x in a if x in b]`
`[(x, y) for x in nums for y in nums]`

steps.hint: Look for loops, including hidden ones: `max`, `sum` and `in` on a list each walk the whole list.
steps.explanation: **O(1)**: indexing a list, a dict lookup and `in` on a set take the same time at any size. **O(log n)**: halving `n` and binary search cut the problem in half each step. **O(n)**: `max`, `sum` and `x in nums` look at every item once; they're loops written for you. **O(n²)**: a loop inside a loop, including the hidden one where `x in b` scans list `b` for each item of `a`. Timed in Python, making n four times bigger left the first five flat (log n grows by just 2 steps), made the middle three about 4× slower and the last two 16× slower or more.

lessons.title: Trading memory for speed
lessons.takeaway: Hash maps buy O(1) lookups with extra memory. Optimize only where n is big — simple beats clever for small inputs.

steps.title: The hash map superpower
steps.body:
A **hash map** (a `dict` in Python, a `Map` in JavaScript) stores key → value pairs and finds a key in **O(1)** on average, no matter how big it gets.

That makes it the most common tool for speeding up code: spend O(n) extra **memory** to avoid repeated O(n) **searches**.

steps.title: Two-sum
steps.problem: Given a list of n numbers and a target, find two numbers that add up to the target.
steps: **Brute force:** check every pair → O(n²) time, O(1) extra memory.
**Better:** walk the list once. For each x, check whether `target - x` is already in a set of the numbers seen so far, then add x to the set.
Each check and insert is O(1) on average, done n times → O(n) time, O(n) memory.
steps.answer: Spending O(n) memory turns O(n²) into **O(n)**. For a million items that's ~10⁶ steps instead of ~10¹².

steps.prompt: You need to remove duplicates from a list of n items. Which approach is O(n) on average?
choices: For each item, scan the result list to see if it's already there
Add items to a hash set, skipping ones that are already in it
Compare every item with every other item
Sort the list, then compare every item with every other item
steps.explanation: Set membership is O(1) on average, so one pass is **O(n)**. Scanning the result list each time is O(n²).

steps.prompt: Another option: sort the list (O(n log n)), then remove adjacent duplicates in one pass (O(n)). What's the total?
steps.explanation: Sequential steps add, and the dominant term wins: O(n log n) + O(n) = **O(n log n)**. A bit slower than hashing, but it can use less memory.

steps.prompt: When is the simple O(n²) brute force perfectly fine?
choices: When n is small (say, a few hundred items) and the simpler code is easier to get right
steps.explanation: 80/20 applies to optimization too: for small n the difference is microseconds. Spend your effort on the code paths that actually handle large inputs.
